content.text: Some mobile phones are recharged at a power point using a charger that contains a transformer. What is the purpose of the transformer?
To convert AC at the power point to DC
To convert DC at the power point to AC
To increase the AC voltage at the power point
To decrease the AC voltage at the power point
A transformer can only induce an emf in the secondary if the flux through the core is changing, so check what a mains power point actually supplies.
A phone needs a small supply voltage, so think about step-up versus step-down and the ratio $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$.
Converting AC into DC is the job of diodes in a rectifier, not of a transformer, so that option describes a different component.
D
A mains power point supplies about 240 V AC, and a transformer only works with an AC input because the changing primary flux is what induces the secondary emf.

A phone needs a few volts, so the charger contains a step-down transformer: with $N_s < N_p$, $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$ makes the secondary voltage a small fraction of the mains voltage. That reduced AC is then rectified by diodes to give the DC needed to charge the battery.
The option about converting AC to DC describes the rectifier, not the transformer, and increasing the voltage would be the wrong direction for a phone charger.

content.text: Both Westinghouse and Edison proposed methods for supplying electricity to homes. What advantage did Westinghouse's method have over Edison's?
DC could be supplied at a lower current, making it safer for the consumer.
DC could be supplied at a lower voltage, making it safer for the consumer.
AC allowed for the use of a lower transmission current, reducing energy losses.
AC allowed for the use of a lower transmission voltage, reducing energy losses.
Compare the two transmission voltages: an AC system can use transformers to raise the voltage for transmission, whereas DC cannot be transformed.
The power transmitted is $P = VI$, so for the same power a higher voltage means a smaller current.
Energy lost in the transmission lines is $P_{\text{loss}} = I^{2}R$, so it is the current that has to be reduced to reduce the losses.
C

Edison's DC system had to be transmitted at a low voltage to be safe to use, so enormous currents were needed to transmit any useful power. With $P = VI$ fixed, a low voltage forces a high current, and the resistive loss in the lines, $P_{\text{loss}} = I^{2}R$, then became prohibitive beyond a few kilometres.

Westinghouse's AC system could use transformers to step the voltage up for transmission and step it down again at the consumer, so for the same power the transmission current was much smaller and the $I^{2}R$ losses in the lines were greatly reduced.
So the advantage is a lower transmission *current*, not a lower voltage - it is the current, through $I^{2}R$, that governs the energy lost on the way to the consumer.

content.text: A region of space contains a constant magnetic field and a constant electric field. How will these fields affect an electron that is stationary in this region?
Both fields will exert a force.
Neither field will exert a force.
Only the electric field will exert a force.
Only the magnetic field will exert a force.
Treat the two fields separately and ask what each one does to a *stationary* charge.
The electric force is $F = qE$ and does not care whether the charge is moving, while the magnetic force is $F = qvB\sin\theta$ and needs a velocity.
With $v = 0$ the sine factor is zero, whatever the strength or direction of the magnetic field.
C
A magnetic field exerts a force $F = qvB\sin\theta$ only on a *moving* charge. The electron is stationary, so $v = 0$ and the magnetic force is zero, no matter how strong the field is.

The electric field exerts $F = qE$ on the electron even at rest, giving an acceleration along the field direction (opposite to the field, since the electron is negatively charged). So the constant electric field is what starts the electron moving.
Only the electric field therefore exerts a force on the stationary electron. Once it is moving the magnetic field will also act on it, but not at the instant described.

content.text: X: Metal, Y: Metal alloy, Z: Compound
X: Metal, Y: Compound, Z: Metal alloy
X: Metal alloy, Y: Metal, Z: Compound
X: Metal alloy, Y: Compound, Z: Metal
Read each circled point as a pair: (year of discovery, critical temperature). The discovery dates are what let you name the actual materials.

Three eras of superconductivity matter here: the first element discovered to superconduct, the record set in the early 1960s by an alloy of two metals, and the 1980s breakthrough with a copper-oxide ceramic. A
X lies at about 1910 with a critical temperature of only a few kelvin. That is mercury, the first substance found to superconduct: a pure element, so a metal.
Y lies at about 1962 at a critical temperature near 20 K. The record in that era was set by niobium tin (Nb$_3$Sn), a material made from two metals, so a metal alloy.

Z lies at about 1986. The first materials to superconduct well above 30 K were the copper-oxide ceramics (lanthanum, barium, copper and oxygen). A ceramic oxide is a compound, not an element and not an alloy.
Only the row X = metal, Y = metal alloy, Z = compound matches all three. The rows that make Y a compound or swap metal with metal alloy misidentify the 1962 alloy or the 1910 element.

content.text: In a thought experiment, a jet is travelling at $0.5c$ relative to the ground, towards a train that is travelling at $0.1c$ relative to the ground, as shown. What is the speed of the light emitted from the train's headlight, as measured by a pilot in the jet?

content.alt_text: Side view of a jet aircraft on a ground line moving to the right with a velocity arrow labelled 0.5 c, and a train on the same ground line moving to the left with a velocity arrow labelled 0.1 c, with a headlight beam projected to the left.

content.text: One postulate of special relativity states that every inertial observer measures the same speed of light in a vacuum, whatever the motion of the source or the observer.
So decide whether Galilean addition of velocities (which would be used for a jet and a train on a road) is valid at these speeds.
D

In a vacuum every inertial observer measures the speed of light as $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, independent of the motion of the source. The train's headlight therefore emits light that the pilot in the jet also measures as travelling at $c$.

Adding the speeds classically would give $0.5c + 0.1c = 0.6c$, and taking the relative speed of the two vehicles would give $0.5c - 0.1c = 0.4c$; both are wrong because velocity addition is not linear at these speeds. The invariance of $c$ is exactly what special relativity requires, so the answer is $1.0c$.

content.text: A magnet passes through a copper tube at constant velocity along the path shown. A current is induced in the tube by the motion of the magnet. Which row of the table correctly describes the forces acting between the tube and the magnet at points P and Q?

content.alt_text: A bar magnet with N pole at the left and S pole at the right approaching the open left end of a horizontal copper tube along a dashed line marked P at the magnet and Q at the far right end, with an arrow labelled 'Path of magnet' pointing right.

content.text: Force at P: Attraction, Force at Q: Repulsion
Force at P: Repulsion, Force at Q: Attraction
Force at P: Attraction, Force at Q: Attraction
Force at P: Repulsion, Force at Q: Repulsion
Lenz's law: the induced current always opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it, so the tube always resists the magnet's motion.
At P the magnet is still approaching the open end, so the flux through the tube is increasing; at Q the magnet is on its way out, so that flux is decreasing.
B

At P the magnet is approaching the copper tube, so the magnetic flux linking the tube is increasing. The induced current flows so as to oppose that increase, which makes the near end of the tube a pole that opposes the approaching magnet: the force at P is a repulsion.
At Q the magnet has almost left, so the flux through the tube is decreasing. The induced current now opposes that decrease by pulling the magnet back, so the force at Q is an attraction.

The row of repulsion at P and attraction at Q is the only one consistent with Lenz's law. It is also why the magnet must be pushed to get through the tube: work done against these forces is dissipated as heat in the tube.

content.text: How does back emf affect a DC motor?
It creates heat in the iron core.
It limits the speed of the motor.
It reverses the current in the coil.
It increases the torque of the motor.
The spinning coil is a conductor moving in a magnetic field, so it induces its own voltage opposing the supply. How does the size of that induced voltage change as the motor speeds up?
Follow that through to the current and then to the torque available from $F = BIl\sin\theta$.
B

As the coil spins it cuts the magnetic field lines, so the flux through it changes and an emf is induced in the coil. By Lenz's law this back emf opposes the supply emf, which is required by conservation of energy.
The faster the coil spins, the faster the flux changes and the larger the back emf, so the net emf across the coil, the current and the driving torque all fall.

The speed therefore settles when the driving torque equals the load torque, which is why back emf limits the speed of a DC motor. It does not reverse the current in the coil (that is the split-ring commutator's job), does not increase torque and does not heat the iron core.

content.text: In a thought experiment, a train is moving at a constant speed of $0.8c$. A lamp is located at the midpoint of a carriage. There are doors W and Z at each end of the carriage which open automatically when light from the lamp reaches them. The passenger standing at the midpoint of the carriage switches on the lamp. Which statement best explains what the passenger observes about the doors?

content.alt_text: Side view of a railway carriage on wheels moving to the right with a velocity arrow labelled 0.8 c, a lamp at the midpoint of the ceiling, a standing passenger beneath the lamp, and doors W (left) and Z (right) at each end.

content.text: Z opens before W because the lamp is moving towards Z.
W opens before Z because W is moving towards the lamp.
W and Z open simultaneously because the lamp is placed at an equal distance from both.
W and Z open simultaneously because the distance from the lamp to each door has contracted by the same amount.
Answer from inside the carriage, where the passenger, lamp and doors are all at rest and the lamp sits at the midpoint.
In that frame light leaves the lamp at speed $c$ in every direction. Compare the distance travelled and the time taken to reach each door.
C

In the carriage's own frame the lamp is at rest at the midpoint, a distance $L/2$ from each door, and the speed of light is $c$. Each door is therefore reached after the same time $t = (L/2)/c$, so both doors open at the same instant.
A and B are wrong because the lamp is not moving relative to the doors at all in this frame, so it cannot reach one door first.

D mentions length contraction, but there is no length contraction to apply in the carriage's own frame; contraction is something a ground observer assigns to the moving carriage. (In the ground frame the lamp is also midway between the doors at the instant it is switched on and light travels at $c$ both ways, so the ground observer also finds the doors opening simultaneously.)

content.text: When light of a specific frequency strikes a metal surface, photoelectrons are emitted. If the light intensity is increased but the frequency remains the same, which row of the table is correct?
Number of photoelectrons emitted: Remains the same; Maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons: Remains the same
Number of photoelectrons emitted: Remains the same; Maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons: Increases
Number of photoelectrons emitted: Increases; Maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons: Remains the same
Number of photoelectrons emitted: Increases; Maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons: Increases
Write Einstein's photoelectric equation $KE_{\max} = hf - \phi$ and ask which of $f$, $\phi$ and the intensity appear in it.
Intensity is about how much energy arrives per second, i.e. how many photons hit the metal each second, not how energetic each photon is.
C

The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is $KE_{\max} = hf - \phi$, which depends only on the frequency of the light and the work function of the metal. Since the frequency is unchanged, $KE_{\max}$ is unchanged when the intensity is increased.
Increasing the intensity at fixed frequency increases the number of photons striking the metal each second, so more photoelectrons are emitted per second.

Hence the number of photoelectrons increases while the maximum kinetic energy stays the same, which is the third row. The rows where the maximum kinetic energy changes wrongly assume the energy of each photon has changed.

content.text: A satellite orbits Earth with period $T$. An identical satellite orbits the planet Xerus which has a mass four times that of Earth. Both satellites have the same orbital radius $r$. What is the period of the satellite orbiting Xerus?

content.alt_text: Two circular orbits of equal radius r: one around a small grey planet labelled Earth and one around a larger grey planet labelled Xerus, each with a satellite drawn on the orbit.

content.text: Use Kepler's third law for satellites, $\frac{r^{3}}{T^{2}} = \frac{GM}{4\pi^{2}}$. Because both satellites have the same orbital radius, work out how $T^{2}$ depends on the central mass $M$.
Quadrupling $M$ divides $T^{2}$ by four. Halve the square first, then take the square root - do not divide the period itself by four.
C
Rearrange Kepler's third law to isolate the period.
With $r$ unchanged, $T^{2} \propto 1/M$, so $T \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$. For Xerus, $M_{X} = 4M_{E}$.

So the period is half the Earth's orbital period. The value $2T$ would be correct if Xerus had a quarter of Earth's mass, and $T/4$ results from dividing $T^{2}$ by four without taking the square root.

content.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the effect of light in a solar cell?
The light produces electron-hole pairs.
The light causes pure silicon to become n-type silicon.
The light increases the potential difference across the p-n boundary.
The light transfers energy to electrons in the conduction band of the p-type semiconductor.
What does the semiconductor do when it absorbs a photon with energy greater than the band gap energy?
Then consider the role of the p-n junction: is the potential difference across it something the light can change, or is it fixed by the doping?
A

A photon with $hf$ greater than the band gap energy promotes an electron from the valence band into the conduction band, leaving a vacancy (a hole) behind. The light therefore produces electron-hole pairs in the semiconductor.

The built-in electric field at the p-n boundary then separates these pairs, driving electrons one way and holes the other, which is the current supplied by a photovoltaic cell. The voltage across the boundary is fixed by the doping, so light increases the current, not the potential difference across the junction, and pure silicon becomes n-type by doping, not by illumination. Electrons are freed from the valence band, not from an already occupied conduction band of the p-type region.

In that frame a projectile feels an effective gravity of $g - a$ rather than $g$. Sketch a parabola for the smaller downward acceleration and compare it with the stationary-lift path.

content.text: Muons are subatomic particles which at rest have a lifetime of $2.2$ microseconds ($\mu\mathrm{s}$). When they are produced in Earth's upper atmosphere, they travel at $0.9999c$. Using classical physics, the distance travelled by a muon in its lifetime can be calculated as follows:
Which row of the table correctly summarises the behaviour of these muons?
Muon's reference frame: distance travelled 660 m, lifetime 2.2 us; Earth's reference frame: distance travelled > 660 m, lifetime > 2.2 us
Muon's reference frame: distance travelled > 660 m, lifetime > 2.2 us; Earth's reference frame: distance travelled > 660 m, lifetime > 2.2 us
Muon's reference frame: distance travelled 660 m, lifetime 2.2 us; Earth's reference frame: distance travelled < 660 m, lifetime < 2.2 us
Muon's reference frame: distance travelled < 660 m, lifetime < 2.2 us; Earth's reference frame: distance travelled 660 m, lifetime 2.2 us
Both observers must agree on the same two events: the muon being produced in the atmosphere and the muon decaying.
In the muon's rest frame its lifetime is the proper lifetime and nothing about it changes. The differences appear in the Earth's frame, where the muon is moving at 0.9999c.
A

In the muon's own frame the muon is at rest, so its lifetime is the proper lifetime $2.2\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and the distance associated with that lifetime at this speed is the classical 660 m. There is no relativistic correction to its own clock.
In the Earth's frame the muon is moving at $0.9999c$, so the Lorentz factor is large.

Time dilation means the Earth's observers measure a lifetime longer than $2.2\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ (about $70.7 \times 2.2 \approx 156\,\mu\mathrm{s}$), and in that longer time at $0.9999c$ the muon travels further than 660 m (about 47 km). Equivalently, the length of the muon-excursion is contracted by the same factor, so both the distance and the lifetime measured on Earth are greater than the classical values.

content.text: In the motor shown, the rotor spins clockwise, as viewed from point P, when connected to a DC supply. What happens when the motor is connected to an AC supply?

content.alt_text: A DC motor drawn in perspective with two field magnets, a rectangular rotor loop on a shaft, a dashed axis of rotation passing through point P, and supply terminals marked minus and plus.

content.text: There is no movement of the rotor.
The rotor produces clockwise movement only.
The rotor vibrates at the frequency of the AC supply.
The rotor continuously turns half a rotation clockwise, then half a rotation anticlockwise.
Look at how the rotor is connected: there is a split-ring commutator, which reverses the current in the coil every half turn so that the torque always acts the same way round.

An AC supply also reverses the current twice in every cycle. Decide whether these two reversals cancel or reinforce each other for the torque, and what the torque does as the current magnitude falls to zero twice a cycle.
B

The motor has a split-ring commutator and brushes. With a DC supply the commutator swaps the coil connections every half turn, so the torque always acts clockwise as viewed from P and the rotor spins continuously.

With an AC supply the current in the coil reverses twice in every cycle, and each of those reversals coincides with the commutator changing which half-ring touches each brush. The two reversals therefore cancel out: the torque remains in the same sense and the rotor still turns clockwise.

What does change is the magnitude of the current, which rises and falls through zero twice a cycle, so the torque and speed ripple at twice the supply frequency while the direction of rotation is unchanged. The rotor neither stops (the current still flows), nor vibrates in one place (the commutator keeps the torque one-way), nor turns a half rotation each way (the torque never reverses).

Now use $a = F/m$. The thrust produced by the gases is roughly constant, so ask what happens to the mass $m$ as the fuel is burnt, and therefore what happens to the acceleration.

The diagram shows the acceleration increasing as the rocket climbs. Remember that the mass loss also reduces the weight, so the net forward force is greater than the thrust alone would suggest, and the trend is even steeper than thrust alone predicts.

The rocket is propelled forwards by expelling gases backwards; the equal and opposite momentum changes of the rocket and the gases conserve momentum, and because the rocket's mass decreases the acceleration increases.

The rocket is propelled forwards by expelling gases backwards. The mutual force acting between the rocket and gases exerts an equal and opposite effect on each. Since this force is applied over the same time interval, the rocket and the gases experience equal and opposite changes in momentum, that is, momentum is conserved.
Since the mass of the rocket is decreasing while the force acting on it due to the gases is constant, the acceleration of the rocket increases as it ascends.

content.text: Explain how different discoveries in physics led to the development of THREE technologies, including the electric generator.
Three technologies are required and one of them is the electric generator, so start each with the discovery and then name the technology that discovery enabled.
For the generator, begin with Faraday's discovery about changing magnetic flux and with the energy source that drives the coil.

For the other two, choose discoveries you can state precisely, such as the deflection of electrons in evacuated tubes or the energy gap in semiconductors and the effect of doping, and make the link to the technology explicit.

Faraday's discovery that a change in magnetic flux induces an emf led to the electric generator; discoveries that electrons could be steered in evacuated tubes led to television; and discoveries about semiconductor energy gaps and doping led to practical computing.
Faraday discovered that a change in magnetic flux would induce an emf in a conductor. This discovery led directly to the development of the electric generator.

Physicists discovered that electrons could be made to travel through evacuated tubes. They were deflected by electric and magnetic fields and could cause a fluorescent screen to emit light. The electrons could be manipulated precisely to form an image on the screen, leading to the development of television.

Physicists made discoveries about the properties of semiconductors. They exhibited a small energy gap between conduction and valence bands that could be altered by doping. Doped semiconductor combinations (eg PNP) formed devices that behaved in the same way as existing thermionic components, allowing the miniaturisation of computers, and the development of practical computing.

content.text: Calculate the maximum possible energy released by the light bulb as the mass falls through a distance of one metre.
The bulb cannot release more energy than the mass loses, so start from the gravitational potential energy $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ and find its change.

Do not use $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: you are on Mars, and the radius $3.4 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$ is what sets the field strength. Either evaluate $U$ at both radii and subtract, or use the fact that over a one-metre drop the change is $\dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}$.
A maximum of $7.48\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy.
The change in gravitational potential energy of the falling mass is the maximum energy that can be released.
This energy is lost by the falling mass, so the light bulb released a maximum of $7.48\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy.

Alternatively, assuming $g_{mars}$ is constant over this range, $W = Fs = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}} \times s = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.39 \times 10^{23} \times 2 \times 1}{3376203^{2}} = 7.48\,\mathrm{J}$.

content.text: Explain the difference in the behaviour of the falling mass when the switch is open.
With the switch closed a current flows in the generator circuit. Ask what that current does to the coil on the iron core and what that implies for the motion of the falling mass.
Now open the circuit and identify which force has disappeared. Use the law of conservation of energy to justify the direction in which the mass's speed changes.
With the switch open the mass falls more quickly, because there is no longer any magnetic effect opposing its fall.

With the switch closed, current flows in the generator and the magnetic field produced opposes the motion of the coil, so energy is transferred to the light bulb and the mass falls slowly. When the switch is open there is no longer any magnetic effect opposing the falling of the mass, so the mass now falls more quickly, as predicted by the law of conservation of energy.

content.text: Answer the following questions about the role of geophysics in exploration and monitoring.
What role do geophysicists play in the monitoring of the nuclear test ban treaties?
For the first sub-part, work strictly in order: what a nuclear explosion produces, what instruments record it, what the record shows, and what decision that allows to be made.
For the second, name the method first, for example a gravity survey, then the anomaly it detects, then what can be extracted as a result, then who benefits.
The benefit has to be an economic one, so link the survey result to an industry or to money rather than stopping at 'finding out where the oil is'.

Nuclear weapon explosions create a unique seismic signature which is detected by seismographs. Geophysicists who analyse the seismograms can deduce whether and where a nuclear explosion has occurred, and so monitor compliance with the test ban treaties.

A nuclear explosion releases an enormous amount of energy in a very short time, which generates a seismic signal with a characteristic origin time, amplitude and magnitude. Because the signal is detectable at great distances on seismographs that are also used to record earthquakes, geophysicists can distinguish an explosion from a natural event and triangulate its location. That is the whole basis of the monitoring: the treaties can be verified only because the physical signature of a test can be detected and located from the recorded seismic data.

content.text: Answer the following questions about the role of geophysics in exploration and monitoring.
Explain how ONE geophysical method used in mineral exploration can produce an economic benefit.

Oil deposits produce gravitational anomalies which can be measured and used to locate the deposits. The oil extracted from these deposits provides energy for a great range of industries, such as transport, so this geophysical method has produced a great economic benefit.

Three links are needed: the method, the anomaly and the benefit. A gravimeter measures the local strength of the gravitational field very precisely, and a deposit of oil or ore of different density from the surrounding rock produces an anomaly in that field. Mapping the anomaly locates the deposit without drilling. The benefit follows because the oil then supplies energy to a great range of industries, and locating a deposit accurately saves the cost of drilling many dry holes. Other acceptable methods include electrical resistivity surveying and magnetic surveys, each with a corresponding economic benefit.

content.text: Answer the following questions about Earth's magnetic field.
For the model, describe it as if Earth contained a bar magnet, and be explicit about where the field lines lie at the equator compared with the poles.
Inclination is measured from Earth's surface and not from the vertical, so describe how that angle changes at the three labelled positions as you move away from the equator.

items: (i) One model that has been used postulates the existence of a permanent dipole, represented as a bar magnet tilted so that its south magnetic pole lies near the geographic north pole. At the equator (B) this model shows Earth's magnetic field being nearly parallel to Earth's surface. As the latitude increases, B to C to D, the inclination of the field to Earth's surface increases, so in the polar regions the field is nearly perpendicular to the surface.

(ii) Earth's magnetic field changes with time, which is observed in the change of position of the magnetic N and S poles over geologically short times. Earth's magnetic field is also not uniformly symmetrical, since it has irregularities that are intrinsic, due to local variations in composition and density, and other irregularities that are extrinsic and change due to effects such as the solar wind.

content.text: (i) A dipole model represents Earth as if a bar magnet lay along its axis, with the south magnetic pole near the geographic north pole and the north magnetic pole near the geographic south pole. The field lines emerge from the northern magnetic pole region and enter near the southern one, outside the Earth. At the equator, point B, the lines are almost tangent to the surface, so the inclination to the surface is close to zero. Moving to higher latitudes, C then D, the lines meet the surface at an increasing angle, so the inclination increases and approaches perpendicularity at the magnetic poles. Three marks require the model, the equatorial case and the change of inclination with latitude.

(ii) Two features are required, neither of which is the latitude dependence just described. First, the field is not static: the positions of the magnetic north and south poles drift over geologically short timescales, so the field itself is changing, and this is what is recorded in the rock record as the magnetic reversals that part (d) uses. Second, the field is not a perfect dipole: the real field is not uniformly symmetrical, showing intrinsic irregularities caused by local variations in the composition and density of the crust, and extrinsic irregularities that come from outside Earth, for example the solar wind interacting with the magnetosphere.

content.text: Explain TWO corrections that must be made when gravimeter data is being analysed.

Name the correction and then give the reason it is needed. The mark scheme requires the reason and not just the label, so one sentence each is not enough.
The two corrections you need are the free-air correction, which deals with height, and the Bouguer correction, which deals with the material between the surface and the sensor.

The free-air correction, for the altitude at which the measurement was taken because gravity decreases with altitude, and the Bouguer correction, for local variations in rock density and distribution.

Analysis of gravimetric data must take the altitude at which the measurement was taken into account since the force of gravity decreases with altitude. Correction for this variable is called the free-air correction.
Corrections must also be applied for local variations in rock density and distribution, since these affect the gravimeter data. This is called the Bouguer correction.

content.text: What valid inferences can be made from these data sets? Justify your answer.

Before inferring anything, establish what is held constant between the two data sets: it is the same mid-ocean ridge, and the same sequence of magnetic reversals in Earth's history has been recorded at both.

Compare the distances from the ridge at which the same band boundaries appear at A and at B. Width divided by time is a rate, so the location where a given reversal interval is compressed into a shorter distance has spread more slowly.
Then check the symmetry of the pattern on each side of the ridge at each location, since that is a separate inference about whether the spreading rate is balanced.
The rate of seafloor spreading at B is slower than at A, and the rate of spreading is the same on either side of the ridge at both locations.

The same patterns of reversal occur over a shorter distance at location B compared with A, so the rate of seafloor spreading at B is slower than the rate at A. This is based on the assumption that the same extrinsic field changes affect cooling rocks at both locations.
The rate of spreading is the same on either side of the ridge at both locations. This is evidenced by the symmetric patterns on either side of the mid-ocean ridge.

The non-uniform width of regions with normal/reverse magnetisation may also be due to variation of the seafloor spreading rate or to variation of the lengths of time between reversals, or both, so further evidence would be required to make a better inference.

content.text: Relate features on the seismograms to the behaviour of different types of earthquake waves and Earth's internal structure.
Each trace should be read as a sequence of arrivals. Identify the wave type of each arrival from the order in which the two wave types must arrive, given their relative speeds.
The gap between the first and second arrival is a distance measure: it is set by how far the station is from the focus, so compare the gaps at W and X rather than the absolute arrival times.
Then use what each wave type can and cannot travel through to say something about Earth's interior, and be especially careful with the station that recorded only a single arrival.

The first event at each station is the faster longitudinal P-wave and the second is the slower transverse S-wave; the greater P-S separation at X shows X is further from the focus; and the absence of an S-wave at Y means no conclusion about a liquid layer can be drawn for that path.

Seismograms at W and X show two events at the stations separated by about 7 minutes and about 11 minutes respectively. The first event in each case is the arrival of the P-waves, followed by the S-wave.

P-waves are longitudinal waves that travel faster than S-waves, which are transverse waves. Since X is further from the earthquake focus, the arrival time difference between P and S waves is greater at X.
S-waves cannot travel through liquids, so there can be no liquid layers extending as far as the line joining the focus and X.

The record at Y only shows the arrival of the P wave, so it cannot be deduced from this record if there is a liquid component between the focus and Y, since we do not know if the S-wave was detected at that location.
The P/S wave records at X have a smaller amplitude than the corresponding waves at W, due to the effect of the inverse square law and absorption of energy by material in the Earth.

content.text: Answer the following questions about X-rays.
What are the differences between hard and soft X-rays?
'Hard' and 'soft' describe the X-ray beam, so compare the two beams on photon energy, wavelength and penetrating power rather than on anything to do with the imaging equipment.
For the second sub-part, list the reasons a clinician would actually choose a plain X-ray for a limb instead of one of the more sophisticated scans, not just the properties of X-rays.
Give reasons rather than facts: 'it is cheap' scores less than 'it is cheap compared with the alternatives, so it is the first investigation performed'.
Hard X-rays have higher energy, and shorter wavelength, than soft X-rays, and consequently a greater ability to penetrate human body structures.

The two differences that carry the marks are the energy of the photons and the distance the beam penetrates body tissue. Hard X-rays have the shorter wavelength, the higher photon energy and the greater penetrating power, so they pass through dense tissue to reach bone. Soft X-rays are absorbed in the superficial layers, which is why they are used for skin and shallow soft tissue.

X-ray imaging provides high contrast between soft tissue and bone, at a resolution sufficient to detect fractures; the technology is cheaper than most alternatives; and it exposes the patient to much less ionising radiation than a CT scan. These are why X-rays are widely used to image human limbs.

Three reasons are needed, each phrased as a reason. First, the diagnostic information required for a limb is structural, and a plain radiograph already gives high contrast between soft tissue and bone at a resolution fine enough to detect a fracture, so a more elaborate scan adds nothing for this presentation. Second, the equipment and the procedure cost far less than the alternatives, so a plain X-ray is the first investigation performed. Third, the ionising dose delivered is much lower than that from a CAT scan, which matters when imaging a common and often minor injury in a large population, especially in children. Each of these must be stated as a reason and not as a bare property to earn the mark.

content.text: Answer the following questions about ultrasound.
Describe the piezoelectric effect and its application in ultrasound imaging.

The piezoelectric effect runs in both directions: a crystal that deforms when a potential difference is applied can also generate a potential difference when it is deformed. Both halves are needed for the mark.

For the second sub-part, write the intensity reflection expression in terms of the two impedances, then evaluate it once for each boundary. One of the boundaries has identical impedances, and that case has to be recognised before any arithmetic is attempted.
Whatever is not reflected is what enters the next medium, so quote both the reflected and the transmitted percentages for the boundary where there is a mismatch.

The piezoelectric effect is the inter-conversion of mechanical and electrical energy in a crystal: a potential difference applied across the crystal makes its shape alter, and conversely applying a force to the crystal results in a potential difference across it. Since these variations can occur at high frequencies, the effect is ideal for creating and for detecting the ultrasound waves used for medical imaging.

The piezoelectric effect is defined as the inter-conversion of mechanical and electrical energy in certain crystals, and both directions must be given. Applying a potential difference across the crystal causes it to deform slightly, and applying a force causes charge to accumulate on its faces, giving a potential difference. Because both the deformation and the charge response can be driven at high frequencies, and the response is rapid and reversible, the effect is ideal for producing the high-frequency pressure variations that are ultrasound, and equally for detecting the returning echo, since a pressure wave striking the crystal generates a voltage that can be amplified.

content.text: Answer the following questions about ultrasound.

An ultrasound pulse leaves the transducer and passes from the gel through soft tissue and bone as shown. A table of acoustic impedances is provided. Describe what happens to the intensity of the ultrasound pulse at each boundary. Use calculations to support your answer.

At the gel to soft-tissue boundary the two acoustic impedances are equal at $1.632\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, so none of the ultrasound pulse is reflected and all of it passes into the soft tissue. At the soft-tissue to bone boundary some of the pulse is reflected and some continues into the bone: $I_r/I_0 = \left(\frac{6.732-1.632}{6.732+1.632}\right)^{2} = 0.372$, so approximately $37\%$ is reflected and approximately $63\%$ passes into the bone.
The fraction of the incident intensity reflected at a boundary between two media is set by the ratio of their acoustic impedances, $Z = \rho c$.

At the first boundary, gel to soft tissue, $Z_1 = Z_2 = 1.632\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, so the numerator is zero and $I_r = 0$. The two media are acoustically matched by the coupling gel, so none of the pulse is reflected at the skin surface and all of it enters the tissue, which is exactly why the gel is used.

At the second boundary, soft tissue to bone, the impedances differ so a large fraction is reflected: approximately $37\%$ of the pulse, leaving approximately $63\%$ to be transmitted into the bone. This large reflection is what produces a strong echo from a fracture, and it is also why bone strongly shadows the structures behind it.

content.text: Contrast the use of Doppler ultrasound imaging with the use of computed axial tomography (CAT) imaging. In your answer, include an example of how each is used.
The command word is 'contrast', so the two techniques must be set against each other on the same criteria: what each one images, and what that lets a doctor do.
An example for each technology is required, and a specific use such as the motion of blood near a valve, or the detection of an abdominal tumour, earns the mark. 'It is used in hospitals' does not.
Keep the distinction sharp: one technique shows how the body is working, the other shows what it is shaped like.

Doppler ultrasound examines functional characteristics such as the motion of body structures and fluids (eg the motion of blood near valves or blockages), whereas CAT examines structural characteristics at very high resolution with excellent contrast (eg detection of abdominal tumours).

Doppler ultrasound is used to examine functional characteristics of the human body, in particular the motion of body structures and fluids. Specific uses include determining the motion of the heart and determining the motion of blood, particularly near valves or blockages.

In contrast, CAT imaging examines structural characteristics of the human body, at very high resolutions. CAT provides excellent contrast between hard and soft tissues, and also different forms of soft tissue. Specific uses include the detection of abdominal tumours and the diagnosis of damaged soft tissue such as cartilage.

content.text: Describe how positron emission tomography (PET) scanning is used in diagnosis. In your answer, refer to the interaction of positrons and electrons.
Follow the sequence in order: what is injected, what it emits, what happens to the emitted particles, what radiation results, and how that radiation is turned into an image.
The question specifically asks about the interaction of positrons and electrons, so name that interaction explicitly and state what it produces.
Then explain why the answer is diagnostically useful: the radiopharmaceutical can be chosen to concentrate in the tissue of interest, so the image is a map of function as well as of position.

A radioisotope that releases positrons is injected; the positrons annihilate with electrons in the body releasing gamma radiation, which is detected by a ring of detectors to map the distribution of the radioisotope.

PET imaging is useful in diagnosis because it allows the use of specific radiopharmaceuticals which can target specific metabolic processes, such as the high rates of metabolism associated with cancerous tissues.

During PET imaging the patient is injected with a radioisotope that releases positrons. These positrons undergo annihilation with nearby electrons in the body, releasing gamma radiation. The patient is surrounded by a circular gamma detector that allows the distribution of the radioisotope within the patient to be computed.

content.text: Explain how principles of physics are applied in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
Start from the physical property of the nucleus that MRI exploits, the spin of the hydrogen nucleus, and state what the strong external field does to the spin directions.
'Resonance' means the applied radiation must match the precession frequency exactly, so say what happens to the nuclei when it does.
Other acceptable physics for later marks: the changing magnetic flux in the detecting coils inducing an emf by electromagnetic induction, and the field coil relying on superconductivity.

Hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnetic field align and precess; a radio wave at the precession frequency is absorbed by resonance and detected by the induced emf in the detecting coils, whose field is produced by superconducting coils.

The physical principles related to spin and resonance are applied in MRI. The magnetic properties of nucleons are related to their spin. Hydrogen is abundant in the human body and has a net spin determined by its single proton. During MRI a patient is placed in a strong magnetic field causing the spin directions of the hydrogen nuclei to align and precess about the magnetic field lines at a specific frequency.

Due to the principle of resonance, a radio wave at this frequency will be readily absorbed by the nuclei, causing their precession to become synchronised and some of them to be placed into a high energy state. This is necessary in order to detect the nuclei in subsequent processes.

Accept also: the principle of electromagnetic induction in the detecting coils; the principle of superconductors in the field coil; and the principles of semiconductor operation in the computers used in MRI.

content.text: Answer the following questions about optical telescopes.
Distinguish between the terms resolution and sensitivity as applied to optical telescopes.
Write one plain sentence for resolution and one for sensitivity, making sure that neither definition is just a rewording of the other.
Ground-based telescopes are limited by atmospheric distortion, so every improvement either compensates for the atmosphere or avoids using it at all.
Two named techniques carry the marks: active or adaptive optics, which corrects the mirror for atmospheric distortion, and interferometry, which combines light from separate collectors.

Resolution of an optical telescope is the ability to distinguish two close objects as separate images. Sensitivity is the light-gathering power, or the ability to detect faint objects for observation, and this depends on the area of the mirror or lens of the telescope.

The two definitions must be clearly different. Resolution concerns the separation of detail in the image, that is, whether two objects that are close together appear as two objects or as one; for a circular aperture it is limited by diffraction. Sensitivity concerns the faintness of the object that can be detected at all, that is, how much light the telescope gathers, and it scales with the collecting area of the mirror or lens. A telescope can therefore be very sensitive and still have poor resolution.

content.text: Answer the following questions about optical telescopes.
Outline ways of improving the resolution of ground-based telescopes.

The resolution of ground-based telescopes can be improved by active optics or adaptive optics, which uses a computer-controlled feedback system to correct the sagging or deformities of the large primary mirror, and by interferometry, which uses data from a number of collectors to produce an interference pattern that is then analysed mathematically to produce a 'less blurred' image.

A star seen through the atmosphere is blurred because the moving air in the atmosphere continually changes the optical path, so the image spreads and moves. Three marks are earned by naming and describing two techniques. Active and adaptive optics use a slow computer-controlled feedback system to measure and then correct for the sagging or deformation of the large primary mirror, correcting in effect for the atmosphere in real time. Interferometry takes a different approach: it combines the light or radio data from a number of separate collectors to produce an interference pattern, which is then analysed mathematically to produce an effectively unblurred image, so the resolution is set by the separation of the collectors rather than by the diameter of any one of them.

content.text: Answer the following questions about determining stellar distances.
Explain how trigonometric parallax is used to determine the distance to a star.

Parallax is an apparent change of position, so the first sub-part is about how the observer's own motion, through the Earth's rotation or its orbit, supplies a measurable baseline against distant background stars.
Use the small-angle relationship to get the distance: with the parallax angle in arc seconds, the distance comes out in parsecs as the reciprocal of the angle.
For the second step, the distance modulus is $M = m - 5\log_{10}(d/10)$. Keep the logarithm in base 10 and put the distance in parsecs.

The apparent position of a nearby star is measured against distant background stars, first from one side of Earth and then, six months later, from the opposite side of its orbit. The resulting angular shift is the parallax angle, and because the baseline, the diameter of Earth's orbit, is known, the distance is calculated as $d = 1/p$ with $p$ in arc seconds and $d$ in parsecs.

(i) The explanation needs the geometry and the measurable shift. Distant stars are so far away that they appear in the same directions from every point on Earth's orbit, so they form a fixed background against which the shift of a nearby star can be measured. Observing the star from opposite sides of Earth's orbit, six months apart, gives a baseline equal to the diameter of the orbit, about $3.0\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, and a small angle between the two apparent positions. This apparent change of position is the parallax angle, and trigonometry on the resulting thin triangle gives the distance directly.

The reciprocal relation holds only because the parsec is defined so that a star with a parallax of one arc second is one parsec away. Viewing positions can also change as Earth rotates, giving a diurnal parallax, but that is far smaller and is not the effect used here.

content.text: Describe how the spectrum of a star can be used to determine its chemical composition and surface temperature.
Two different pieces of information come out of one spectrum, so treat the identification of composition and the measurement of temperature as separate steps.
For composition, the key word is absorption: the dark lines are produced by the atoms in the star's atmosphere absorbing particular frequencies of the light passing through them.
For temperature, ask which species the lines belong to: molecules, neutral atoms and ionised atoms each appear only within particular temperature ranges.
Absorption lines identify the elements and molecules present, and the presence of molecules, neutral atoms or ionised atoms gives the surface temperature.
Particles in the atmosphere of stars absorb specific frequencies of light, allowing the elements and molecules to be identified. Hence chemical composition can be determined.
The presence of molecules, neutral atoms or ionised atoms in a star are determined by its temperature. These can be detected in the absorption spectrum, allowing their temperature to be deduced.

content.text: Describe how the distribution of stars on a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram relates to the processes that occur during their evolution.
Identify the three populated regions of the diagram, the main sequence, red giants and white dwarfs, and the energy source that sustains each.
Then account for the empty space: a star passes through the transition between two processes very quickly compared with the time it spends in each group.
A sketch of the diagram with the regions labelled, together with the process for each, will pick up more marks than the processes alone.

Stars cluster into the main sequence, red giants and white dwarfs, corresponding to hydrogen fusion, helium fusion and gravitational collapse respectively, with few stars in between because the transitions are quick.
Stars on an H-R diagram are non-uniformly distributed into distinct groups dependent on processes which occur during their evolution.

The primary source of energy in stars on the main sequence is hydrogen fusion. In the next evolutionary stage for most stars, helium fusion is the main source of energy. These belong to the group known as red giants.

The next evolutionary stage for most stars is characterised by gravitational collapse during which gravitational potential energy is converted to radiant energy. These belong to the group known as white dwarfs.
Since the transition from one process to another occurs quickly relative to the time spent in each group, fewer stars are distributed in areas outside of these groups on the H-R diagram.
Accept also: reference to other groups such as protostars and supergiants, a sketch of the H-R diagram, and globular and open clusters.

content.text: Answer the following questions about nucleons.
Explain the stability of He-4 nuclei in terms of TWO forces.

Protons carry a positive charge, so there is electrostatic repulsion between the protons in the nucleus. The strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together: it occurs between proton-proton, neutron-neutron and proton-neutron pairs, and is strongly attractive when the nucleons are $0.5$ to $1.0$ times a proton diameter apart, which is the separation in a $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus. Anything outside that range becomes repulsive, so at the separation in helium the attraction outweighs the repulsion and the nucleus is stable.

Three marks require both forces, each correctly attributed, plus the balance. The electrostatic force is repulsive between like charges, so the two protons in a $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus repel each other and on its own would drive the nucleus apart. The strong nuclear force acts between all pairs of nucleons, proton-proton, neutron-neutron and proton-neutron, and is by far the strongest force at nuclear distances. Crucially it is strongly attractive only when the nucleons are separated by $0.5$ to $1.0$ times a proton diameter, and becomes repulsive outside that range. The two protons and two neutrons in a $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus sit within that window, so the strong attraction between all four nucleons outweighs the electrostatic repulsion between the two protons, and the nucleus is stable. This also explains why the helium nucleus is tightly bound compared with the energy that would be needed to separate its nucleons.

The extension worth adding is that the strong force has a very short range. In a larger nucleus most protons are further apart than that range, so the strong force cannot hold them all against their mutual repulsion; extra neutrons are needed to add strong-force attraction without adding repulsion, and beyond a certain point even that is not enough, which is why large nuclei become unstable.

content.text: (i) Two features are required. The second is the hyperfine structure: with more sensitive instruments, extra lines are resolved close to the main lines, and these can only be explained if the energy level itself is split into slightly different sub-levels, for example by the interaction between the electron spin and the proton spin. content.text: Describe how contributions to atomic theory made by Pauli and Heisenberg changed Bohr's model of the atom.
Take each scientist in turn: state the principle, then state the specific change it forced on Bohr's picture of the electron.
For Pauli, the change concerns how many electrons a shell can hold. For Heisenberg, it concerns how precisely the electron's position and its momentum can be known at the same time.
Because the question says the contributions changed Bohr's model, a change must be stated for each; naming the principle alone earns only the partial marks.
Pauli's exclusion principle limited the number of electrons in each shell, and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle replaced Bohr's fixed shells with orbital probability clouds.

Pauli introduced the last quantum number associated with spin. His exclusion principle states that no two electrons can have the same quantum number. This changed Bohr's model by limiting the number of electrons that can exist in each shell.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that if you know the accurate position of the particle then you cannot know its momentum accurately, and vice versa. This changed Bohr's shell to an orbital probability cloud since precise measurements cannot be made.

An analogue output is a continuous waveform, a smoothly varying voltage whose value at any instant is proportional to the input. A digital output is a square wave that takes only two discrete values, a high and a low level, so it carries information as a stream of two states.

An analogue output follows the input continuously, so the trace is a smooth curve and any voltage between the extremes is possible at some instant. content.text: Answer the following questions about operational amplifiers.
Build a table with one row for each property, voltage gain, input impedance, output resistance and bandwidth, and fill in the ideal value, the real value and the comparison.
For the circuit, identify which input terminal carries the signal: an inverting amplifier sends the input through a resistor to the inverting terminal, with the non-inverting terminal grounded.

items: (i) This op amp does not have ideal properties. An ideal amplifier has infinite open-loop voltage gain and infinite input impedance, while this op amp has a very high but finite gain of $200\,000$ and a finite input impedance of $2\,\mathrm{M\Omega}$. An ideal amplifier has zero output resistance, while this op amp has a relatively low but not insignificant output resistance of $100\,\Omega$. An ideal amplifier has infinite bandwidth, while this amplifier has a limited bandwidth of $0$ to $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$.

(ii) The circuit is an inverting amplifier: $V_{in}$ through $2.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ to the inverting input, the non-inverting input grounded, and an $11\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor from the output back to the inverting input, giving a gain of $-11/2.2 = -5$.

content.text: (i) Three marks require all four properties compared, each phrased as a comparison with the ideal case. The ideal amplifier is a limiting case: infinite open-loop voltage gain so that even a tiny differential input saturates the output, infinite input impedance so that no current is drawn from the source, zero output resistance so that the output voltage does not drop when a load is connected, and infinite bandwidth so that all frequencies from zero to infinity are amplified equally. The real op amp differs on every count: $200\,000$ is very large but finite, $2\,\mathrm{M\Omega}$ is very large but finite so a small current is drawn, $100\,\Omega$ is low but not zero, and the $0$ to $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ bandwidth means frequencies above $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ are attenuated.

(ii) The two graphs show the output inverted and five times larger than the input, with the peaks of $+2\,\mathrm{V}$ on the input corresponding to $-10\,\mathrm{V}$ on the output. That fixes the gain at $-5$, and the gain of an inverting amplifier is set by the ratio of the two resistors, so the feedback resistor follows directly from the given input resistor.

The circuit must therefore be drawn with the $2.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ input resistor between $V_{in}$ and the inverting terminal, the non-inverting terminal connected to ground, and the $11\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ feedback resistor bridging from the output terminal back to the inverting terminal. The negative sign of the gain is what identifies it as inverting, and the magnitude $-5$ is what sizes the feedback resistor. A common error is to place the feedback resistor from the output to the non-inverting terminal, which would give positive feedback and saturate the op amp.

content.text: A circuit is required to automatically switch on a 240 V fan when the temperature exceeds 30 degrees C. The circuit shown was designed by a student but does not operate as intended.

content.text: The graph shows the characteristic curve of the thermistor in the circuit.

content.alt_text: Graph of resistance (100 to 100 000 ohm, logarithmic scale) against temperature (0 to 80 degrees C), falling from about 20 000 ohm at 0 degrees C to about 700 ohm at 80 degrees C.

content.text: Explain THREE changes that need to be made for this circuit to operate correctly.
The op amp has no negative feedback here, so it acts as a comparator: it switches when its input voltage reaches the reference set by $R_2$ and $R_3$.

Calculate that reference voltage and then the input voltage the divider actually reaches at $30^{\circ}\,\mathrm{C}$. If the two can never be equal, no component value is doing its job, and one of them must be wrong.
Then check the direction: with a PTC thermistor, does the input voltage rise or fall as the temperature rises, and is that the behaviour the fan needs?
Use a relay in place of the fan; change R1 to 5 k-ohm; and swap the positions of R1 and the thermistor.

Use a relay - the fan is stated as 240 V. This would require a current and voltage greater than what can be supplied by an electronic circuit. In this case a relay should be used in place of the fan and the fan can be driven by a separate circuit through the relay.

R1 should be 5 k-ohm - an op amp in open loop configuration will act as a comparator. It will switch between high and low when the input voltage equals the reference voltage. In this case the reference voltage is 7.5 V due to R2 and R3 being equal. However the input voltage will never match this as R1 is too great. To match 7.5 V, R1 should equal the required thermistor value. From the graph the thermistor will be 5 k-ohm at 30 degrees, so R1 should also be 5 k-ohm.

Swap the positions of R1 and the thermistor. Since the resistance decreases with temperature, an increase in temperature will tend to pull down the input voltage. This means the fan will be on below 30 degrees and switch off above 30 degrees, which is the opposite of what is required. Swapping R1 and the thermistor would rectify this.
Accept also: adjusting the reference voltage by changing the values of either R2 or R3 to suit the R1/thermistor voltage divider, or swapping the two inputs of the op amp.
